title: Chapter 199 – Little Mei's Questions
html:
[The Mother Tree and the Kitchen Loft – Mei]

Little Mei wants to know why the sky is so far away.

It is the first thing she says in the morning, before she has opened her eyes, before she has found her rabbit, before Mei has even finished sitting up on the narrow bench in Qinghe's loft. The question comes out of the quilt in a clear small voice, with the grave unhurried tone of a child who has been waiting all night to ask it.

"It isn't far," says Mei. "It's only high."

"It's higher than it was."

"Was it?"

"At home it was only up to the roof." A pause, rustling. "Now it goes all the way to the stars."

Mei looks at the small lump under the quilt. She is learning not to answer too quickly. She has had six days of this, six mornings of questions, and she has found that the child does not want the first answer, or the second. She wants the real one, and she can tell the difference.

"It's higher because you're outside," she says at last. "At home you were inside a house. Here there's no roof. There's only the Hall, and the valley, and the sky, and it goes up forever."

"Forever's a long time."

"Yes."

"Is that why the grown-ups are tired?"

Mei's throat tightens. She reaches over and smooths the rumpled brown hair, very gently, and feels the warmth of the little head under her palm. She cannot do that, really. Her hand is light, not flesh, and it passes through more often than it touches. But the leaf in her pocket hums when she tries, and for a moment she can feel the hair, soft and slightly damp, between her fingers.

"Partly," she says.

"What's the other part?"

"They had a lot of things to hold. And nobody to help."

"Now there's me," says Little Mei.

She says it so simply that Mei does not answer at all.

* * *

Breakfast is a crowded affair.

The kitchen is full of the Seven, and of Hua, who sits at the end of the long bench with her daughter pressed against her side and a bowl of porridge growing cold in front of her. She looks better than she did a week ago. Qinghe has found her a gown that fits, and she has pinned up her gray-shot hair with a bone comb, and the sharp schoolmistress face has softened at the corners. She watches Mo Yan eat with an expression of fierce, careful attention, as if memorizing each mouthful.

"She eats like Duan Ke," says Hua, to no one in particular.

"I do not," says Duan Ke.

"Quickly, and as though someone might take it."

The boy flushes. Tao, beside him, giggles through a full mouth.

Bell stands at the stove with a small stool, and on the stool, with her legs swinging, sits Little Mei. The healer holds the child's wrist in two dry fingers and counts. Her lips move. Her eyes are narrowed.

"Well?" says Qinghe, from the pot.

"Strong." Bell lets go. "Strong as a pony. Pulse good, lungs clear, eyes bright. I have not seen a child so healthy since I came to the valley."

"But?"

"There is no but." Bell hesitates. "Only a small thing. Her hands are cold."

"I'm always cold," says Little Mei.

"In the fingertips. More than the rest." Bell turns the small hand over and presses the nail of the thumb, and the pink goes white, and takes a long breath to return. "It's nothing. A little slow. I'd keep her in the warm."

"I don't like the warm," says the child, with dignity. "It's too much."

"You may have a quilt."

"I don't like quilts."

"Then you may sit by Mo Yan and be insufferable," says Bell, and lifts her off the stool. "I'll look again tomorrow."

Mei watches from the corner. She does not say anything. But as the child scampers back to the bench, she finds that she has put her hand to her own chest, where a heart would be, and that she is counting.

They climb the hill together in the thin cold light, hand in hand.

Or not quite hand in hand. Little Mei walks with her right hand tucked into the crook of Mei's elbow, because it is the only part of her that Mei can hold for more than a moment, and she carries Mr. Ear under her other arm like a loaf of bread. She wears a gown of Qinghe's cut small, of undyed wool, tied at the waist with a bit of kitchen twine. She has refused shoes. Mei, who spent a hundred years on a floor of cold glass, understands and says nothing.

The orchard is white with frost. The ice on the Mother Tree's branches rings softly in the wind, a hundred little bells, and the lullaby comes down through the silver boughs like warm rain. At the foot of the great trunk the root cellar's lid lies open on the snow. Nobody has closed it. Nobody has dared.

Little Mei stops at the edge of the hollow and looks down the stair.

"It's dark," she says.

"Yes."

"It's not scary." She tilts her head. "It's sad."

"You can tell?"

"The big voice isn't there. It used to sing to me. Now there's only the stair." She wriggles her hand free and walks forward on her bare feet, and Mei, with a lurch of her heart, follows. The child kneels at the lip of the cellar. She lays her small palm flat on the frozen earth. Her face goes quite still.

"He's sleeping," she says.

"Who is?"

"The big voice. He said he was going to dream about fields." A small satisfied nod. "He's dreaming about a field. It's yellow. It has a river."

"How do you know?"

"I can hear."

Mei kneels beside her. The snow soaks through her light, but she does not feel it. She lays her own hand on the earth next to the child's, thin and silver and almost transparent, and closes her eyes. She tries to listen.

She hears nothing. A faint slow warmth, perhaps, the pulse of the Mother Tree's roots. The deep still quiet of a thing at rest. Not a field. Not a river.

"I can't hear it," she says.

"You're too loud."

"I'm what?"

"You're thinking too much." Little Mei opens one eye. "Papa said you always did. He said when you were five you'd stand in the kitchen and think so hard the milk turned sour."

A startled laugh comes out of Mei before she can stop it. It is the first she has made in days.

"Did he really?"

"He said you took after Mama."

* * *

At midday she goes down to the Long Gallery, because it is her turn at the ring.

It is the second waking day. The gauze is hung again. The lamps stand in their rows. A new thousand are stirring, a little ragged, a little afraid, in the grip of the same cold morning that drew the first. The Nine sit in their circle with their hands joined, and Mei takes the ninth stool, and the golden flame trembles into life on the low black table.

She is better at it than she was. She can feel the difference. Where the first day had been like dragging a boat across sand, today is more like rowing. She finds the threads easily, each one thin and gold and attached to a lamp, and she tells them softly, in the voice that is not a voice, wake, if you wish to wake, and she watches them take the offer, one by one.

Perrin Ado sits at the far end of the gallery, apart from the rest.

She can see him from her stool. He is still in his gray gown, with a blanket round his shoulders, and he has refused soup, refused company, refused the offer of a bed. He sits on a bench against the wall with his back straight and his black eyes fixed on the gauze, and he has been there since dawn. Hai Ren sits two benches away with her slate on her knee, writing every word he says.

"He talks in his sleep," says Jian, softly, at Mei's ear.

She turns her head. The Head of the Lin clan has taken the stool beside her, and he looks, if possible, thinner than he did yesterday. The hand that holds hers is cold and steady. The tremor she has learned to see is gone, for now.

"Does he?"

"Last night, for an hour. He named three people. All dead, I think. And a place." Jian's mouth tightens. "He said, the stair goes up and does not stop."

"That's what the note said. Come up."

"Yes." He looks down at the golden flame. "The Tenth. A man's voice. A man who went up and has been calling for six hundred years."

"Why now?"

"Because we opened Door Seven." He sounds very tired. "I think it was always going to be an answer. We did not stop to think about whom."

She presses his hand. She does not know what else to do. The flame between them gutters and rights itself.

"Whatever it is," she says, "we'll be nine."

"We will."

"All ten," says Mei, and smiles. "If you count Little Mei."

His own smile is brief and crooked. Then it fades. He is looking past her, across the gallery, at the Archivist on his bench.

"She is not on the Roll," he says. "She is not on any list. She has no lamp."

"She's a person."

"I know. But the Interface..." He stops, and shakes his head. "I am sorry. I should not trouble you."

"What about the Interface?"

"It does not know what to do with her." He says it very quietly. "She has a body. She has a pattern. She is a child of your father's, and a child of the Bloom's, and neither of them has told it what she is. It marks her UNCLASSIFIED."

Mei feels a chill. She says nothing.

"I thought you should know," says Jian.

The afternoon belongs to Nurse.

She has taken Little Mei under her wing with the grim tenderness of a woman who has waited six centuries to be allowed. They sit together at the end of the kitchen table, the old nurse and the barefoot child, with a basket of wool between them. Nurse's needles click. The child watches them with her chin on her fist.

"You hold it like this," says Nurse. "The loop goes over. And under. And through."

"Why?"

"So it doesn't come undone."

"But what if it does?"

"Then you pick it up again." Nurse smiles. It is a small tired smile, and Mei, in her corner by the stove, sees that it is the first she has seen on that round face in a year. "That is the whole of knitting, child. Everything else is decoration."

Little Mei takes the needles. She holds them like two sticks. The wool snarls and puckers in her fingers, and she scowls ferociously, and Nurse, with infinite patience, reaches over and straightens each loop without a word.

"You were at the hospital," says the child, abruptly. "When I was small."

Nurse's hands stop.

"Mei said. Papa said. You were my nurse."

"I was."

"Did I like you?"

A long silence. The fire pops. Nurse puts down the wool, very carefully, and looks at the child's grave upturned face.

"You bit me," she says. "Twice."

"Why?"

"You were four, and I had a needle." Her voice cracks on the laugh. "I do not blame you. I should have bitten me too."

Little Mei considers. "I'm sorry."

"There is nothing to be sorry for."

"I'll try not to do it again."

"Please do," says Nurse. She wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist and picks the wool up again. "But you may bite me once more, if you like. For old times' sake."

The child giggles. It is a high, silvery, delighted sound, and it fills the kitchen. Mei, in her corner, presses her fingers to her lips and cannot say a word.

She wants to know about you, says Lena, from the tree. She asks me every night.

It is evening, and the sun has gone, and the two of them are curled together at the foot of the great silver trunk with the rabbit between them. Little Mei is asleep. She fell asleep in the middle of a sentence, with her cheek on Mr. Ear and one hand clenched in Mei's sleeve, and she has not moved since. Her breath rises and falls like a small slow tide.

What do you tell her? says Mei.

That you're the bravest person I know.

That isn't true.

Nonsense. The branches stir, and a shower of ice falls softly through the dark. You sat with a dying boy and never told him to stop. You held a door for a hundred years with nothing but a song. You said no to a better body when it was offered to you. I do not know what else you would call that.

Stubborn.

Both. A warm rustle, like a laugh. You were stubborn at five, too. I had the greatest trouble getting you to wear shoes.

Mei looks down at the sleeping child. At the bare dirty feet tucked under the hem of the gown. A tide of something rises in her chest, so strong and unexpected that she has to press her hand to her mouth.

She has no shoes, she whispers.

She does not like them.

I never liked them either. Her eyes sting. I just forgot.

You did not forget. You were told, and you believed it.

Told what?

That you were a copy. The voice is very gentle. That the real girl was gone. That what remained was only a pattern. The roots shift under the snow, and a warm light runs along them, from the trunk to the toes of Mei's boots. Mei. Look at her. Look at her feet. She is five, and she is barefoot in the snow, and she is not cold. She has not been told to wear shoes since the day she was born. She is a copy of nothing. She is a child who was kept in the dark by a creature that did not know how to stop, and who woke up with her own feet.

Mama, says Mei.

It is the first time she has said it aloud. She did not know she was going to. It slips out of her like a drop falling from a branch, and she hears it ring against the bark.

Yes, my love.

What if she's the real one?

Then she is the real one. The voice does not waver. And you are the one who stayed. And we are both mine, and you are both yours, and no one has to be a copy of anybody. That is the first thing I mean to teach her. You are the second.

Mei laughs. It comes out wet. She wipes her face with the back of her hand and feels the warmth of the leaf in her pocket, and the weight of the child against her side.

Teach me what?

Rest, says Lena. You are at four and a half percent, and you have not slept in a week.

I don't need to.

Everyone needs to. Even a keystone. The branches lower, slowly, until the silver twigs lie in her lap like a blanket. Sleep, Mei. I will keep the lamp.

She wants to argue. She finds that she cannot find the words. The warmth is too great and too kind, and the hum of the lullaby has risen round her like a tide. She leans her head against the trunk. Her eyes close.

She does not dream. But for the first time in a hundred years, she sleeps.

* * *

She wakes to a small hand shaking her shoulder.

It is dark, and very cold, and for a moment she does not know where she is. The stars are fierce and close through the bare branches. The tree is silent. Beside her the quilt where Little Mei lay has been flung back, and the rabbit is gone.

"Mei," says a small voice. "Mei, wake up."

She is on her feet before she knows it. The child stands in front of her in the snow, barefoot, with her hair in her eyes and Mr. Ear dangling by his single ear from her fist. She is shivering. Her face in the starlight is very white.

"What is it?"

"I did something," says Little Mei. "I didn't mean to."

"What did you do?"

"I tried to help." Her lip trembles. "I heard the ring. The big one, the one in the Hall. It was like a bell that was too quiet. I thought, I could make it louder. And then I did."

Mei does not breathe.

"Show me," she says.

The child holds out her hand. In the starlight it looks perfectly ordinary, small and brown and a little dirty. But as Mei watches, a fine thread of pale gold light rises from the palm, thin as a hair, and hangs in the air, and she feels the pull of it all through her, down to her toes.

It is a thread of the Nine-Ring.

It is her thread. The one that leaks. The one that, for a week, she has felt thinning, little by little, with every day that she held the Hall's lamps. It runs from her chest to the child's hand, taut and shining, and along it, steadily, like water along a wick, flows something warm.

"You're lending me," she whispers.

"Is that bad?"

"How much?"

"A little." The small face crumples. "It wasn't hard. It just came. You were so tired and I thought, I have lots. I'm new. I don't need all of mine."

"How much, Little Mei?"

"Two." A pause. "Two and a bit."

Mei's knees give way. She sits down in the snow. She sits with the thread still humming between them, and the cold goes through her like a blade, and she understands, all at once, that she is at six and a half percent, and that she was at four and a half when she fell asleep. She understands that the child has been lending her steadily for hours, in the dark, while she slept. She understands what it means to have a body that can give.

"It's good," says Little Mei, anxiously. "Isn't it? You look better."

"I do."

"Then why are you crying?"

Mei cannot answer. She reaches out, and the child steps into her arms. For one breath, for two, the light of her hands holds. She feels the small warm back under her fingers, the thumping heart, the heat of a living child who has done a thing she does not know the price of.

"Because I'm not allowed to," she says into the brown hair. "I'm not allowed to take this. You're five. It isn't yours to give."

"Why?"

"Because it costs."

"But I have lots."

"Not as much as you think."

She feels the child go still. The warm thread goes slack between them. She looks down.

The small face is turned up to hers, perfectly white, with the eyes enormous and strange. A fine tremor runs through the thin shoulders. The lips are blue.

"Mei," says Little Mei, in a voice like a pulled thread. "My hands feel funny."

The rabbit falls into the snow.

"Mei, my hands—"

She is shaking now, the whole small body, with the quick rattling shiver of something breaking. Mei catches her as she falls. The child is light, so light, and fiercely hot, as if lit from inside. The thread of gold is brightening, flaring, pouring itself back into her palm.

"Help," says Mei.

No one hears.

"Help," she screams, in a voice she did not know she owned, and the whole orchard rings with it. The ice on every branch shatters at once in a silver rain. Down the hill, in the dark, a door bangs. A voice shouts. The Mother Tree begins to sing, wildly, a high cracked song of fear, and Mei holds the burning child against her chest and screams again and again into the cold, while the stars wheel and the roots tremble under her knees.

They come running.

She hears them before she sees them, a pounding of boots on frozen ground, a shouted name, a light swinging wildly through the trees. Tian Mo reaches her first. He takes the orchard slope in six enormous strides with the lantern in his stone hand, and when he sees the child he does not ask a single question. He falls to his knees in the snow and puts his palm flat against the small chest, and a warm green light runs from the roots of his arm into her ribs.

"Breathing," he says, hoarse. "She is breathing."

"The fault," says Mei. "It's the fault."

"I know."

"I did it. I didn't stop her. I was asleep, and she was lending me—"

"Hush." He lifts the child into his arms as though she were made of glass. "Not now. Run ahead. Fetch Bell."

"I can't—"

"You can." His eyes meet hers, black and level in the lantern light. "You are six and a half percent. You can run to the kitchen. I will follow."

She runs. The snow clings to her light, and every step costs a hundredth she does not have, and she does not stop. Behind her she hears the Warden's slow tread and the child's thin rattling breath. Ahead, at the foot of the hill, a window is yellow with firelight. A door bangs open. Qinghe is there in her nightgown with a lamp, and Jian behind her, gray-faced, with his staff, and Bell, half-dressed, with her black bag already in her hand.

"Where?" says Bell.

"Up there. The Warden's carrying her."

"What happened?"

"She lent me," says Mei. The words tear out of her in a sob. "She lent me hers. I didn't know."

Bell does not stop. She runs, small and brisk, up the hill, with the bag banging at her hip, and Jian watches her go. He stands in the doorway for one breath, with the lamplight on his face, and Mei sees his left hand begin to shake.

He sees her seeing it. He does not hide it.

"Come," he says, and holds out the other.

She takes it. He has no strength to spare, and she has less. They climb the hill together, leaning, two tired things in the dark, and at the top, in the heart of the broken ice, they find Tian Mo kneeling with the child's head on his stone arm. Her eyes are open. They are fixed on the stars. Her lips move.

"Mama," whispers Little Mei, to the tree.

It is not a fever. Mei knows it at once, with the cold, clear certainty of a thing she has read about in her father's notes a thousand times.

It is the blood fault. The first sign. At five years old, in the snow, beside a girl who has been dead for six hundred years, the sickness that killed her has finally come for the one who lived.

Above them the Mother Tree sings on, high and cracked and unafraid, and the ice that fell from its branches lies in glittering heaps across the hill. Mei kneels in it with Jian's cold hand in hers, and for the first time since the night in the basement, she does not know what to do.

"Bring the lantern closer," says Bell, behind her, in a voice with no expression at all. It is the voice of a healer who has seen the worst and is deciding how to say it. "I need to see her hands."
